items.title: Concept: tests that check side effects, and Goal/Check exercises
items.body:
The tests in `tests/boundaries.test.mjs` import the real modules and pass in a fake provider: a small function that returns a known value or throws. That lets a test count how many times the "provider" was called. 04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md explains why the count matters: an error status is not enough if a paid request was already made.

The practice chapters use a **Goal / Check** pattern. The Goal says what should be true after a change. The Check is a concrete action whose result proves it: a test assertion, a DevTools command, or a click in the UI. A good Check tests exactly that goal and would fail if the goal were not met.

When a quiz gives you a Goal and four Checks, read each Check and ask: what does this action exercise (which file, which function)? Does that match the code the Goal names? Checks from other tasks are often good checks, just for a different goal.

excerpts.quote: The [test file](../tests/boundaries.test.mjs) imports actual production modules, so changing the parser or orchestration changes the tested behavior.
Keep your answers beside test output so you can distinguish a prediction from something you learned after running the program.

items.title: Why the parser does not catch butter in a vegan recipe
items.body:
Read the recipe-ingredient part of `parseRecipe`. For `isFromUser` it only checks `typeof item.isFromUser !== "boolean"`: it must be true or false. It does not compare the name with the user's ingredient list. Nothing in this code looks at diet either. So butter marked `isFromUser: true` in a vegan request passes, as long as the shape and numbers are valid. The guide says it plainly: "The parser verifies shape and arithmetic, not truth."

Why the others are wrong:
- No code compares dietary choices with ingredient names.
- No code matches `isFromUser` ingredients against the request list.
- `allowMissingOne` only controls how many recipes may have a `missingIngredient`; it does not turn on name matching.

excerpts.quote: const ingredients = list(recipe.ingredients, "Recipe ingredients", 1, 30).map((value) => { const item = record(value, "Recipe ingredient"); if (typeof item.isFromUser !== "boolean") throw new Error("Invalid ingredient origin."); return { name: text(item.name, "Ingredient name", 100), amount: number(item.amount, "Ingredient amount", Number.MIN_VALUE, 10_000), unit: text(item.unit, "Ingredient unit", 40), isFromUser: item.isFromUser, }; });

Notice what is **not** checked: that `isFromUser: true` ingredients actually appear in the user's list, or that a "vegan" request produced vegan recipes. The parser verifies shape and arithmetic, not truth.

const missingCount = recipes.filter((recipe) => recipe.missingIngredient !== null).length; if (missingCount > (input.preferences.allowMissingOne ? 1 : 0)) throw new Error("Too many recipes with a missing ingredient.");

items.title: Goal "unique favourites across generations": which check shows it
items.body:
The model invents recipe ids, and the parser only checks that ids are distinct *within one batch*. Two different batches can both contain `"recipe-1"`. Favourites are looked up by recipe id, so the second "recipe-1" can collide with the first. The Goal is to make favourites unique even then.

The matching Check builds exactly that situation: two batches whose first recipes share id `"recipe-1"` but have different titles. Both can be favourited, and `getFavorites()` returns 2 items. - the `decodeRecipe(...)` is `null` check belongs to "Validate share links".
- the sessionStorage `currentResult` check belongs to "Validate the results page".
None of them creates two batches with a repeated id.

items.title: What the browser gets after two unparseable provider replies
items.body:
Each attempt calls `parseRecipes(await generate(input), input)` inside a try. If parsing throws, the `catch` does nothing except a comment: "Provider error details must not be exposed to the browser." After two failed attempts the loop ends and the function returns `{ status: 500, body: { error: "Couldn't generate recipes right now. Please try again later." } }`. That is a fixed text, the same every time. No parser message or provider output is added.

Why the others are wrong:
- The status is 500, not 502, and the raw provider reply is never included.
- An empty 200 never happens; 200 is returned only with recipes that passed the parser.
- The parser's message is caught and thrown away, so it is not in the body.

excerpts.quote: // Preserve the previous maximum of two attempts, including malformed provider output. for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 2; attempt++) { try { const recipes = parseRecipes(await generate(input), input); return { status: 200, body: { recipes } }; } catch { // Provider error details must not be exposed to the browser. } } return { status: 500, body: { error: "Couldn't generate recipes right now. Please try again later." } };

items.title: Why "body as {...}" did nothing about a null body
items.body:
`as` in TypeScript is a type assertion. It tells the compiler "treat this value as this type". It produces no code that runs: after compilation, `body as { ingredients: unknown; ... }` is just `body`. So when the JSON body was the literal `null`, nothing checked it; the original code went on with `null`. The guide: an assertion "does not inspect the expression at runtime". The fix is a real runtime check: `record()` throws "... must be an object." when the value is `null`, an array or a primitive.

Why the others are wrong:
- An assertion never creates or changes values, so no empty object appears.
- It cannot throw, because no assertion code exists at runtime.
- `null` is valid JSON, so decoding it succeeds; the guide says the assertion "did not prevent `body` from being `null`".

excerpts.quote: A TypeScript assertion says how the compiler should treat an expression. It does not inspect the expression at runtime.

function record(value: unknown, name: string): RecordValue { if (value === null || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) { throw new Error(`${name} must be an object.`); } return value as RecordValue; }

items.title: Goal "prove the injection seam": which check shows it
items.body:
A **seam** is a place where you can swap one piece for another without editing the code. `generateRecipeResponse(body, generate)` takes the provider as its second argument, a function. That argument is the injection seam: you can pass any function, including a fake that throws.

The matching Check calls `generateRecipeResponse` directly with valid input and `async () => { throw new Error("x") }` as the provider, and observes `{ status: 500 }` with no `recipes` key. That proves the seam: you controlled the provider from outside, and the function reacted as designed, with no real network call. The guide pairs this Goal with exactly this Check.

Why the other Check does not fit: the "returns `[{}]` first, then a valid batch" Check is for the next exercise, "see the retry count". It also uses a fake provider, but what it proves is the number of attempts (call counter 2, status 200), not the seam itself.

items.title: Goal "validate the results page": which check shows it
items.body:
Today `app/results/page.tsx` reads `sessionStorage.currentResult` and only runs `JSON.parse` on it, inside a try. Valid JSON with the wrong shape, such as `{"recipes":[{}]}`, gets through, and the page then tries to render it. The Goal is to also pass it through `parseGenerationResult` and redirect home when that fails.

The matching Check puts exactly that bad value in sessionStorage from DevTools and loads `/results`. If the goal is met, the parser rejects it, the catch runs `router.replace("/")`, and you land on `/` with no console error. The Check targets the same page and storage key the Goal names.

- the 20-chips check belongs to "Cap ingredients in the UI" (`IngredientInput.tsx`).
- the `decodeRecipe(...)` is `null` check belongs to "Validate share links" (`lib/share.ts`).
- the two `"recipe-1"` batches check belongs to "Stop favourite-id collisions" (history ids).

items.title: Why the rate limiter stops honest users but not attackers
items.body:
`checkRateLimit(ip)` counts requests per key in a `Map` and refuses after 10 per minute. The key comes from `request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")`, a header the client can set to anything. An honest user always sends the same value (or none), so they hit the limit. An attacker just sends a new made-up value with each request, and each one starts a fresh count. Review finding 4 adds two more limits: the `Map` never evicts old keys, and on serverless each instance has its own `Map`. It is rated Medium because each request that gets through can cost a paid provider call.

Why the others are wrong:
- The limiter runs in `POST`, the handler that generates recipes.
- A success does not reset the count; only time past `resetAt` does.
- There is no API key; the key is the forwarded-for header.

excerpts.quote: function checkRateLimit(ip: string): boolean { const now = Date.now(); const entry = rateLimitMap.get(ip); if (!entry || now > entry.resetAt) { rateLimitMap.set(ip, { count: 1, resetAt: now + 60_000 }); return true; } if (entry.count >= 10) return false; entry.count++; return true; }
export async function POST(request: NextRequest) { const ip = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() || request.headers.get("x-real-ip") ||
Rate limit keyed on client-controlled `x-forwarded-for`; `Map` never evicts; per-instance on serverless. It limits honest users, not attackers.

items.title: Concept: where untrusted data becomes trusted
items.body:
Data that comes from outside your program (an HTTP body, a model's reply, a string in browser storage) has type `unknown` in honest code: you do not yet know its shape. The app's job is to turn it into the trusted types in `lib/types.ts` at one clear place, called a **boundary**.

01-CODEBASE-MAP.md has a table "Where each type is trusted". For each value it says where it arrives and the exact function whose return value can be trusted. For example, the HTTP body arrives as `unknown` in the route and becomes trusted only when `parseGenerationInput` returns.

Use that table as a checklist. For any value in a quiz, ask:

- Where does it enter?
- Which function checks it, if any?
- What happens when the check fails: an error status, a retry, or skipping one record?

The parsers are built from four small helpers in `lib/validation.ts` (`record`, `text`, `number`, `list`). 02-CONCEPTS.md lists what each one accepts and rejects; read that table before the quizzes.

excerpts.quote: | Value | Arrives as | Becomes trusted at | | --- | --- | --- | | HTTP body | `unknown` (`route.ts:106`) | `parseGenerationInput` returns (`lib/validation.ts:58-66`) | | Provider output | `unknown` (`route.ts:74-76`, return type `Promise<unknown>`) | `parseRecipes` returns (`lib/validation.ts:117`) |

items.title: Why one 45-minute recipe fails a 30-minute request
items.body:
`parseRecipes` first checks each recipe's shape. Then, when it is given the accepted `input`, it runs cross-field rules. One is `recipes.some((recipe) => recipe.totalMinutes > input.timeLimit || ...)`: if any recipe takes longer than the limit, it throws "Recipes must respect the requested time and servings." The whole batch fails, not one recipe. In the orchestrator, that throw is caught as a failed attempt, so a second attempt may run.

Why the others are wrong:
- No recipe is dropped; the batch must be exactly three valid recipes.
- Being well-formed is not enough; the cross-field rule checks fit to the request.
- No value is changed (clamped); the parser only accepts or throws.

excerpts.quote: if (input) { if (recipes.some((recipe) => recipe.totalMinutes > input.timeLimit || recipe.servings !== input.preferences.servings)) { throw new Error("Recipes must respect the requested time and servings."); } const missingCount = recipes.filter((recipe) => recipe.missingIngredient !== null).length; if (missingCount > (input.preferences.allowMissingOne ? 1 : 0)) throw new Error("Too many recipes with a missing ingredient."); }
- every `totalMinutes ≤ timeLimit` and every `servings` equals the requested servings (`:111-113`);

items.title: Why " Rice" and "rice " count as the same ingredient
items.body:
Each ingredient goes through `text(item, "Ingredient", 100)`. `text` checks that the value is a non-blank string and returns `value.trim()`, so " Rice" becomes "Rice" and "rice " becomes "rice". Then the distinctness check builds `new Set(ingredients.map((item) => item.toLowerCase()))`. Both become "rice", the Set has size 1 but the list has 2, and the parser throws "Ingredients must be distinct." The orchestrator turns a parse error into a 400 with that message.

Why the others are wrong:
- Both values have real letters, so `text` accepts them; the whitespace is trimmed, not rejected.
- The raw strings differ, but the comparison is made after trimming and lowercasing.
- The parser never removes duplicates quietly; it throws.

excerpts.quote: function text(value: unknown, name: string, maximum: number): string { if (typeof value !== "string" || !value.trim() || value.trim().length > maximum) { throw new Error(`${name} must be non-empty text of at most ${maximum} characters.`); } return value.trim(); }

const ingredients = list(input.ingredients, "Ingredients", 2, 20) .map((item) => text(item, "Ingredient", 100)); if (new Set(ingredients.map((item) => item.toLowerCase())).size !== ingredients.length) { throw new Error("Ingredients must be distinct."); }

items.title: Goal "see the retry count": which check shows it
items.body:
The orchestrator allows two attempts: `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 2; attempt++)`. To *see* that number you need a provider whose first reply is bad and whose second is good, and you count the calls.

The matching Check does exactly that. The fake returns `[{}]` first (which `parseRecipes` rejects) and a valid batch second. The call counter ends at 2 and the status is 200, as in the test at `tests/boundaries.test.mjs:84-88`. It then asks you to change the loop bound to `1` and watch that test fail. That makes the retry visible from both sides: with it you recover, without it you do not.

Why the other Check does not fit: the "always throws" Check belongs to "prove the injection seam". A provider that always fails gives a 500 whether there are one or two attempts, so on its own it cannot show how many retries happen.

items.title: Why an extra "injected" field never reaches the provider
items.body:
`parseGenerationInput` does not return the object it was given. It ends with a new object literal that lists only named fields: `ingredients`, `timeLimit`, and `preferences` with its four fields. Any other property, like `injected: "ignored"`, is simply never copied. The provider receives only this new object. The test proves it: it sends a request with `injected: "ignored"` and asserts `deepEqual(seen, input())`, so what the provider saw equals the clean input exactly. It also expects status 200.

Why the others are wrong:
- The field is gone before the provider is called; `parseRecipes` deals with the provider's reply, not the request.
- The request is not rejected: the test expects 200, so extra fields are dropped quietly.
- The field does not pass through; the new object has no place for it.

excerpts.quote: return { ingredients, timeLimit, preferences: { dietary, servings: number(prefs.servings, "Servings", 1, 6, true), skillLevel: prefs.skillLevel, allowMissingOne: prefs.allowMissingOne, }, };

test("valid request is normalized without retaining unknown fields", async () => { const request = { ...input(), ingredients: [" rice ", "beans"], injected: "ignored" }; let seen; const response = await generateRecipeResponse(request, async (value) => { seen = value; return recipes(); }); assert.equal(response.status, 200); assert.deepEqual(seen, input()); assert.deepEqual(response.body.recipes, recipes()); });

items.title: Why one bad recipe fails the batch but one bad history entry does not
items.body:
The two collections mean different things. A provider response is one new batch of three recipes, made just now for one request. It must meet the whole contract: `parseRecipes` requires exactly three, each valid, with distinct ids. A partly valid batch is not a correct answer to the request, so it fails (and the orchestrator may retry). Saved history is different: each entry is a separate record the user already owns. Losing every record because one is broken would hurt the user, so each one is checked alone. The guide says the difference comes "from ownership and user expectations".

Why the others are wrong:
- The guide says directly that it is not "an arbitrary preference for throwing errors or catching exceptions".
- Retry cost is not the reason given; the history read is not retried at all.
- Storage code can throw (`JSON.parse` can), which is why the read uses try/catch.

excerpts.quote: Compare fail-fast and recover-partially behavior. A provider response is one new generated collection and must satisfy the complete contract. Existing history is a collection of independent records, so partial recovery is useful. The policy difference comes from ownership and user expectations, not from an arbitrary preference for throwing errors or catching exceptions.

export function parseRecipes(value: unknown, input?: GenerationInput): Recipe[] { const recipes = list(value, "Recipes", 3, 3).map(parseRecipe); if (new Set(recipes.map((recipe) => recipe.id)).size !== 3) throw new Error("Recipe IDs must be distinct.");

items.title: Start here: the recipe app's boundaries and the course order
items.body:
This pack uses a small Next.js recipe app and a short course about it in `astraupskill/`. The user picks ingredients, a server asks a model provider for three recipes, and the browser keeps history and favourites.

Read the course in the order its README gives:

1. **01-CODEBASE-MAP.md**: the request path from the form to the API route to `lib/generation.ts`, and the "Line-by-line route map" table. Keep this open as your map.
2. **02-CONCEPTS.md**: runtime contracts, the four parser primitives in `lib/validation.ts`, cross-field rules, and when to fail, retry or recover.
3. **03-WORKED-CHANGE.md**: the change that added validation, line by line, plus two Goal/Check exercises.
4. **04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md**: what `tests/boundaries.test.mjs` checks and its blind spots.
5. **05-PRACTICE.md**: tasks, each with a **Goal** (what to change) and a **Check** (how you know it worked). Try them before reading on.
6. **07-TRACE-LAB.md**, then **06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md** last, as its name says.

For every quiz, open the line numbers the course gives and read the actual code.

items.title: Why a crafted share link crashes the shared recipe page
items.body:
`decodeRecipe` decodes the link and returns `JSON.parse(json) as Recipe`. The `as Recipe` is only a type assertion; it checks nothing at runtime. `{"title":"x"}` is valid JSON, so no exception happens and the `catch` (which returns null) never runs. The page gets a non-null "recipe" without an `ingredients` array, skips the "not found" branch, and `SharedRecipeClient` calls `recipe.ingredients.map` on `undefined`: a crash. Review finding 1 describes exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing fills in defaults; the object is used as it is.
- `decodeRecipe` returns null only if decoding or `JSON.parse` throws, and here neither does.
- `parseRecipe` is not called inside `decodeRecipe` yet; adding it is the fix in practice task "Validate share links".

excerpts.quote: export function decodeRecipe(param: string): Recipe | null { try { const decoded = decodeURIComponent(param); const json = decodeURIComponent(escape(atob(decoded))); return JSON.parse(json) as Recipe; } catch { return null; } }

items.title: The parser trims text and converts nothing else
items.body:
Look at what each helper returns. `text` returns `value.trim()`, the only change to any value. `number` first checks `typeof value !== "number"`, so the string "2" fails right away and throws "... must be an integer from 1 to 6." (for servings). It never calls `Number(...)` or `parseInt`. So the only normalisation is trimming; a numeric string is rejected. The guide: "Normalisation is limited to trimming."

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing lowercases values on the way out. The `toLowerCase()` in the ingredient check is only used to compare for duplicates; the returned ingredients keep their case.
- Strings like "2" are rejected, not parsed into numbers.
- It is not "no change at all": text is trimmed.

excerpts.quote: function text(value: unknown, name: string, maximum: number): string { if (typeof value !== "string" || !value.trim() || value.trim().length > maximum) { throw new Error(`${name} must be non-empty text of at most ${maximum} characters.`); } return value.trim(); } function number(value: unknown, name: string, min: number, max: number, integer = false): number { if (typeof value !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(value) || value < min || value > max || (integer && !Number.isInteger(value))) { throw new Error(`${name} must be ${integer ? "an integer" : "a finite number"} from ${min} to ${max}.`); } return value; }
- **Normalisation is limited to trimming.** `text` trims, nothing else coerces. `"2"` for servings is rejected rather than converted (`:24-29`).

items.title: Why reading history keeps good entries and leaves storage alone
items.body:
`readValidItems` parses the stored JSON, checks it is an array, and then runs `flatMap` over the entries. For each one it tries `parse(item)`: a good entry becomes `[entry]`, a bad one throws and becomes `[]`. `flatMap` joins these lists, so the two good entries come back and the two bad ones disappear from the result. The function only reads; it never calls `setItem`. The guide says it returns accepted records "without rewriting the stored string during a read", so rendering a page can never delete data by accident.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing is written back during the read.
- Bad entries are dropped, not returned with a flag.
- One bad entry does not empty the list; each entry is checked on its own.

excerpts.quote: /** A corrupt entry must not hide unrelated valid learning history. */ function readValidItems<T>(raw: string, parse: (value: unknown) => T): T[] { const value: unknown = JSON.parse(raw); if (!Array.isArray(value)) return []; return value.flatMap((item) => { try { return [parse(item)]; } catch { return []; } }); }
validates entries individually and returns only accepted records, without rewriting the stored string during a read.

items.title: Why a string "2" for servings costs zero provider calls
items.body:
In `generateRecipeResponse`, `parseGenerationInput(body)` runs first, inside its own try/catch. The servings check uses `number(..., integer)`, which rejects the string "2". The catch returns `{ status: 400, ... }` at once. The retry loop, the only place `generate(input)` is called, comes after that return, so the provider is never called. The guide: "A malformed request should result in zero provider calls", and placing parsing before the loop means "retrying cannot turn invalid input into a paid request."

Why the others are wrong:
- The retry loop never starts, because the function has already returned.
- "2" is not converted; `number` rejects anything that is not a real number.
- The provider is not asked even once; the check that fails is on the request, not on the provider's output.

excerpts.quote: let input: GenerationInput; try { input = parseGenerationInput(body); } catch (error) { return { status: 400, body: { error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Invalid request." } }; } // Preserve the previous maximum of two attempts, including malformed provider output. for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 2; attempt++) { try { const recipes = parseRecipes(await generate(input), input);
The [orchestrator](../lib/generation.ts) places parsing before its retry loop, so retrying cannot turn invalid input into a paid request.
